en: Rough and harsh; causing irritation in manner
hook: ABRASIVE: like sandpaper SCRAPING.
story: Abrasive. On her first day at a bank in Motijheel, Mitu met the branch manager, a man who corrected people by shouting across the floor and answered every question with a sneer. Within a month, three clerks had asked for transfers. Everyone agreed he was competent but abrasive: harsh and irritating in manner, rubbing people the wrong way. The word comes from abrasion, the scraping of sandpaper on wood. An abrasive cleaner scratches a pot; an abrasive personality scratches feelings. Synonyms: caustic, grating.

gre.s: Though his insights were often brilliant, the critic's ____ manner alienated many colleagues, who found his relentless sarcasm exhausting.
gre.clue: who found his relentless sarcasm exhausting

example: The new captain's abrasive style unsettled the squad, and by midseason several senior players had stopped speaking to him.

en: To quiet someone's anger, often by granting what they want
bn: তুষ্ট করা; দাবি মেনে শান্ত করা
hook: APPEASE: give them 'A PEACE' offering so they stop fighting.
story: Appease. In the supermarket, four-year-old Babu threw himself on the floor and screamed for chocolate. Shoppers stared. His mother, red-faced, grabbed a chocolate bar from the shelf and handed it to him. The screaming stopped instantly. Babu smiled. Lesson learned: screaming works. To appease is to calm someone by giving in to their demands. In history, leaders who appeased aggressive dictators often encouraged even more aggression. Think: give them a peace offering.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ the striking workers, management offered a modest raise, though it refused their central demand for shorter hours.
gre.clue: management offered a modest raise

example: To appease fans furious about the cancelled concert, the organisers promised full refunds and a free show the following spring.

en: Confident and forceful in stating one's views or rights
hook: ASSERTIVE: firmly ASSERTS what she wants.
story: Assertive. At the end of a successful project, Sara's manager prepared to present it to the board, with his own name on every slide. Sara walked into his office. "I led this project for six months. I would like my name on the report, and I would like to present the results myself." She stayed calm and polite, but she did not back down. She was assertive: confident and forceful in stating her views or rights, without being aggressive.

gre.s: Once timid in meetings, the young analyst became increasingly ____, confidently defending her proposals against senior colleagues.
gre.clue: confidently defending her proposals against senior colleagues

example: A short course in negotiation helped Farzana become more assertive when asking clients to settle their overdue invoices.

en: To increase the size or amount of something
hook: AUGMENT: like AUGMENTED reality adding layers to the world.
story: Augment. Tanvir's tuition fees swallowed most of his monthly allowance, leaving almost nothing for books. So he began teaching mathematics to two schoolchildren in the evenings. The extra eight thousand taka a month augmented his income enough to buy his GRE prep books. To augment is to make greater by adding to. You can augment a salary, a collection, or a team. Augment shares a Latin root with the name Augustus: augere, to increase. Synonyms: increase, supplement, boost.

gre.s: Because her scholarship barely covered tuition, she took a part-time job to ____ her income, adding enough each month to pay the rent.
gre.clue: adding enough each month to pay the rent

example: The museum augmented its small collection of Mughal miniatures with a generous loan from a private collector.

en: A picture or description that exaggerates features for comic effect
hook: CARICATURE: a CARtoon that exaggerates.
story: Caricature. At the Ekushey book fair, a street artist drew Arif in two minutes for fifty taka. The drawing gave him an enormous head, a huge toothy grin, and glasses the size of dinner plates, yet everyone recognised him instantly. It was a caricature: a picture or description that exaggerates features for comic effect. Political cartoonists draw caricatures of leaders. The word comes from the Italian caricare, to load or overload. Synonyms: parody, lampoon, burlesque.

gre.s: The novel's portrait of the professor is less a realistic character study than a ____: his vanity is so inflated and his absent-mindedness so extreme that no reader could mistake him for a real person.
gre.clue: no reader could mistake him for a real person

example: The film reduces the scientist to a caricature, a wild-haired genius who mutters equations and forgets to eat.

en: Done in secret, usually because it is not allowed
hook: CLANDESTINE: a secret CLAN meeting in the DESTINY hour of midnight.
story: Clandestine. During the 1971 war, freedom fighters met in village huts at midnight, whispering plans by the light of a single candle. Messages were hidden in rice sacks and passed by children who looked like they were playing. If discovered, everyone would be arrested or worse. Their meetings were clandestine: secret, hidden, usually because they are forbidden. A clandestine operation, a clandestine affair. Think of a secret clan meeting under the stars.

gre.s: The two rival companies held ____ talks for months, keeping the negotiations hidden even from their own boards of directors.
gre.clue: keeping the negotiations hidden even from their own boards

example: Customs officers uncovered a clandestine workshop in Chattogram where fake medicines were packed into genuine-looking boxes.

en: Self-satisfied and unaware of possible dangers or shortcomings
hook: COMPLACENT: so COMfortable in their PLACE that they stop trying.
story: Complacent. After scoring 318 on his first practice test, Arif felt brilliant. He stopped reviewing vocabulary. He played video games every evening. "I've got this," he told everyone. On the real test, he scored 301. Overconfidence had made him careless. He had become complacent: smugly self-satisfied, unaware of dangers and weaknesses. Complacency is the enemy of success. Think: so comfortable in your place that you stop trying.

gre.s: Having won the championship three years in a row, the team grew ____, skipping practices and underestimating opponents they once feared.
gre.clue: skipping practices and underestimating opponents

example: Years without a serious flood had made the town's officials complacent, and the drains had not been cleaned in a decade.

en: Making a certain outcome likely; helpful
hook: CONDUCIVE: CONDUCTS you toward a result.
story: Conducive. Sara could never study in her family's crowded flat in Mirpur, with the television blaring and cousins dropping by. So she found a corner of the university library: soft light, a big window, total silence. In that corner she finished two chapters in one afternoon. The library was conducive to study: it made good work likely. Conducive means making a certain outcome likely, or helpful to it, and it is usually followed by to. Think: it conducts you toward a result.

gre.s: Critics argued that the open-plan office, with its constant chatter and interruptions, was hardly ____ to the deep concentration that serious research demands.
gre.clue: with its constant chatter and interruptions

example: Warm, humid air is highly conducive to the growth of mould, so archivists keep old manuscripts in cool, dry rooms.

en: To have a mutual relationship in which one thing affects or depends on another
hook: CO-RELATE: RELATED together.
story: Correlate. Researchers surveyed a thousand GRE students. They found that hours of sleep correlated with test scores: students who slept more tended to score higher. But did sleep cause the higher scores? Or were organised students simply better at both sleeping and studying? Correlation is not causation. To correlate is to have a mutual relationship in which one thing changes along with another. GRE arguments love to test this trap.

gre.s: Although rates of the two diseases tend to ____, researchers have found no evidence that one actually causes the other.
gre.clue: researchers have found no evidence that one actually causes the other

example: In the survey, the number of trees on a street correlated closely with how safe residents felt walking there at night.

en: Clever at achieving goals through deceit
hook: CRAFTY: CRAFTS clever tricks.
story: Crafty. A street vendor at Gulistan sold Farhan a pair of imported sunglasses, swearing they came from Italy. He even produced a receipt and a shiny box. Farhan paid triple the usual price. At home, he peeled off the sticker and found the words "Made in Chawkbazar" underneath. The vendor was crafty: clever at getting what he wants through tricks and deceit. In folk tales, the fox is the classic crafty animal. Synonyms: wily, sly, cunning.

gre.s: The ____ negotiator concealed his true objectives behind a show of friendly candor, leading his rivals to concede far more than they had ever intended.
gre.clue: concealed his true objectives behind a show of friendly candor

example: In the old folktale, a crafty jackal persuades the crocodile gripping his leg that it has only caught a tree root.

en: Contemptibly cowardly
hook: CRAVEN: the opposite of a brave RAVEN, it flies away at any danger.
story: Craven. On a crowded street, a thief snatched an old woman's bag and ran. A tall young man standing right beside her saw everything. He looked at the thief, looked at the woman, then turned and walked away, pretending he had noticed nothing. Shopkeepers who saw him spat on the ground. His behaviour was craven: shamefully, contemptibly cowardly. Craven is stronger than scared. A craven leader abandons others to save himself.

gre.s: Historians have judged the general's retreat as ____, since he abandoned his troops at the first sign of danger.
gre.clue: abandoned his troops at the first sign of danger

example: The board's craven silence, while the founder bullied junior staff for years, shocked investors when the truth finally came out.

en: So harmful that it leaves someone weak or unable to function
hook: DE-BILITATE: removes your ABILITY.
story: Debilitating. When Mitu caught dengue, the fever lasted a week. The weakness lasted a month. She could not climb the stairs to her flat without stopping twice. She could not hold a book for more than ten minutes. Even her favourite food tasted like cardboard. The illness was debilitating: causing serious weakness and making normal life impossible. Debilitating migraines, debilitating anxiety, debilitating injuries. Think: it removes your ability.

gre.s: For years she suffered from ____ migraines, which sometimes confined her to a dark room for days at a time.
gre.clue: confined her to a dark room for days at a time

example: A debilitating shortage of trained nurses forced the rural hospital to close two of its four wards.

en: To publicly declare something wrong or evil
hook: DE-NOUNCE: ANNOUNCE it's bad.
story: Denounce. At a public meeting, the headmistress of a village school stood up in front of the elders and the local chairman. She announced that a powerful family had been marrying off fourteen-year-old girls, and declared that it was illegal and wrong. She had denounced the practice: publicly declared it wrong or evil. Denounce can also mean to inform against someone, as in denouncing a traitor. The noun is denunciation. Synonyms: condemn, decry, censure.

gre.s: Human rights groups were quick to ____ the arrests, calling them a blatant attempt to silence the government's most outspoken critics.
gre.clue: calling them a blatant attempt to silence the government's most outspoken critics

example: The football federation denounced the racist chanting from the stands and fined the home club heavily.

en: To take apart; to gradually end a system
hook: DIS-MANTLE: remove the MANTLE (covering) piece by piece.
story: Dismantle. Kamal's old car finally stopped running. Instead of selling it whole, he and his cousin spent a week dismantling it in the yard: wheels in one pile, seats in another, the engine on a plastic sheet. They sold every part separately. To dismantle is to take apart piece by piece. It also means to end a system gradually, as when a new government dismantles an old law. Dis means apart; think of stripping a mantle, a cloak, away. Synonyms: disassemble, demolish.

gre.s: The new administration promised not merely to reform the corrupt licensing system but to ____ it entirely, replacing the old agency with an independent commission.
gre.clue: not merely to reform the corrupt licensing system

example: After the festival, volunteers dismantled the bamboo stage in a single night and stacked the poles neatly for next year.

en: Fluent, persuasive, and expressive in speaking or writing
hook: E-LOQU-ENT: 'loqu' means speak. Speaks beautifully.
story: Eloquent. At the inter-college debate, a shy first-year student from a village school spoke last. She talked for only three minutes, about her mother, who sold vegetables on the roadside to pay for her books. Her words were simple, but so moving that the judges stopped writing and the hall fell silent. She was eloquent: fluent, persuasive, and expressive. Eloquent comes from Latin loqui, to speak, as in loquacious. Even a silence can be eloquent. Synonyms: articulate, expressive, persuasive.

gre.s: Though the senator was famously awkward in live debates, his written speeches were remarkably ____, moving even his opponents with their clarity and grace.
gre.clue: moving even his opponents with their clarity and grace

example: Her eloquent letter to the city council, describing the children who played beside an open drain, won funding for a covered sewer.

en: No longer close or friendly with someone; separated
hook: ESTRANGED: became STRANGERS.
story: Estranged. Two brothers in Comilla once shared a bed, a bicycle, and every secret. Then their father died, and a bitter quarrel over land began. For ten years they did not speak. They skipped each other's weddings, their children grew up as strangers, and their mother cried every Eid. They had become estranged: once close, now separated and unfriendly. Estranged means turned into strangers. It usually describes family members or spouses who have drifted or broken apart.

gre.s: After decades of silence, the ____ siblings were finally reconciled at their mother's bedside.
gre.clue: After decades of silence

example: The novel follows an estranged father and daughter who are forced to share a car on a long drive across Spain.

en: Lacking physical strength; weak and unconvincing
hook: FEEBLE: sounds weak, like a FEEBLE 'meh'.
story: Feeble. After two weeks of dengue fever, Tanvir's grandfather was so feeble that he could not lift a glass of water. Tanvir held it to his lips. That same week, Tanvir missed an assignment deadline and told his professor that his dog had eaten his laptop. He does not have a dog. The professor sighed at such a feeble excuse. Feeble means lacking physical strength, or weak and unconvincing. A feeble attempt barely tries.

gre.s: The company's ____ response to the crisis, a single vague press release issued a week late, only deepened customers' anger.
gre.clue: a single vague press release issued a week late

example: Rakib's feeble excuse that a goat had eaten his homework only made the teacher laugh.

en: Not serious; silly or unimportant
hook: FRIVOLOUS: FREE-and-VOLUME-less, no weight, no seriousness.
story: Frivolous. Tanvir received a scholarship stipend of twenty thousand taka for books. Within a week he had spent it on a gaming skin, a phone cover with lights, three milkshakes, and a hat he never wore. When the semester began, he could not afford a single textbook. His spending had been frivolous: silly, unimportant, lacking serious purpose. A frivolous lawsuit has no real legal basis. A frivolous person treats important things lightly.

gre.s: The judge dismissed the lawsuit as ____, noting that the plaintiff had suffered no harm whatsoever.
gre.clue: had suffered no harm whatsoever

example: The committee wasted an hour on frivolous questions about napkin colours while the real budget problem went undiscussed.

en: Made of parts that are all alike; the same throughout
hook: HOMO = same, GENE = kind. Same kind all through.
story: Homogeneous. Priya's mother stood over the cake batter, stirring and stirring. "Not yet," she said. "I can still see lumps." She kept going until every spoonful looked exactly the same: smooth, golden, no streaks of flour anywhere. "Now it is homogeneous." Homogeneous means uniform throughout, made of parts that are all alike. Homo means same, genus means kind. Its opposite is heterogeneous, which means mixed and varied, like a fruit salad.

gre.s: Once thought to be culturally ____, the region turns out to have been a patchwork of distinct languages and customs.
gre.clue: turns out to have been a patchwork

example: Geologists drilled cores at several points to check whether the rock layer was homogeneous or held pockets of other minerals.

en: Causing harm slowly and quietly, so it is hard to notice
hook: INSIDIOUS: sneaks INSIDE you quietly.
story: Insidious. High blood pressure is often called the silent killer. Arif's father felt perfectly healthy for years while the pressure was quietly damaging his heart and kidneys. By the time any symptoms appeared, the harm was serious. The disease was insidious: proceeding gradually and subtly, but with harmful effects. The Latin root means to lie in wait, as in an ambush. Rumours, too, can spread insidiously. Synonyms: stealthy, subtle, treacherous.

gre.s: The danger of the pollutant lies in its ____ nature: it accumulates in the body slowly and without symptoms, causing irreversible harm long before it can be detected.
gre.clue: slowly and without symptoms

example: Office gossip can have an insidious effect on a team, slowly eroding trust until colleagues stop sharing ideas.

en: Twisted together; closely connected
hook: INTER-TWINED: TWINE twisted together.
story: Intertwined. Behind Priya's grandmother's house stand two old trees, a mango and a jackfruit, planted on the same day sixty years ago. Their branches have grown around each other so closely that nobody can say where one ends and the other begins. They are intertwined: twisted together. The word is often used for lives and ideas too: in Bangladesh, the histories of the language movement and independence are deeply intertwined, closely connected. Synonyms: entwined, interwoven, interlinked.

gre.s: In the novelist's vision, the fates of the two families are so ____ that no misfortune can befall one without eventually striking the other.
gre.clue: no misfortune can befall one without eventually striking the other

example: Behind the television, the cables had become so intertwined that tracing a single wire took Kamal half an hour.

en: Anger
hook: IRE: IRATE = angry.
story: Ire. The bus conductor in Mirpur charged Kamal double fare and then refused to give back his change. Kamal's face went red, his voice rose, and he refused to get off until the money was returned. The conductor had aroused his ire: his anger. Ire is a short, literary word for anger, and it gives us irate, meaning very angry. Newspapers love it: a decision draws the ire of critics. Synonyms: anger, wrath, indignation. Its opposite is calm or approval.

gre.s: The new tax on mobile data drew the ____ of students across the country, who staged noisy protests outside the ministry for an entire week.
gre.clue: staged noisy protests outside the ministry

example: Leaving dirty dishes in the hostel sink is the surest way to earn the ire of Mrs Akter, the strict warden.

en: Showing great attention to detail; very careful and precise
hook: METICULOUS: METIC-ulous, every metric measured perfectly.
story: Meticulous. Before every exam, half of Joya's class lines up to borrow her notes. Each page is colour-coded: blue for definitions, green for examples, red for exceptions. Every diagram is labelled. Every margin holds a summary. There is not a single crossed-out word. Her notes are meticulous: showing extreme care and attention to detail. A meticulous surgeon leaves nothing to chance. Synonyms: scrupulous, painstaking, punctilious.

gre.s: The restoration took six years because the conservators were ____, cleaning the fresco one square centimeter at a time.
gre.clue: cleaning the fresco one square centimeter at a time

example: A meticulous tailor in Old Dhaka measured my father twelve times before cutting a single inch of cloth for his wedding suit.

en: Covered with a great deal of fancy decoration
hook: ORNATE: full of ORNAMENTS.
story: Ornate. Inside Ahsan Manzil, the old pink palace beside the Buriganga, visitors stare up at painted ceilings, gilded mirrors, carved wooden doors, and chandeliers dripping with glass. Every surface seems decorated. The palace is ornate: elaborately decorated, sometimes to excess. Ornate shares a root with ornament. Writing can be ornate too, full of flowery phrases and long, decorated sentences. Opposite: plain, austere. Synonyms: elaborate, lavish, florid.

gre.s: Critics accustomed to the novelist's spare, plain prose were surprised by the ____ style of his memoir, with its long, flowery sentences and extravagant metaphors.
gre.clue: with its long, flowery sentences and extravagant metaphors

example: The bride's ornate jamdani sari, woven with silver thread, took two weavers in Narayanganj almost four months to finish.

en: So intense or obvious that it can almost be touched or felt
hook: PALPABLE: you can PALPATE it, touch it with your hand.
story: Palpable. In the coaching centre, forty students waited for their official GRE scores to load on the screen. Nobody spoke. Nobody moved. Someone's leg bounced nervously under a desk. You could almost reach out and touch the tension in the air. It was palpable: so intense or obvious that it can almost be physically felt. Doctors palpate, or touch, a body to examine it. Palpable relief, palpable excitement, palpable fear.

gre.s: As the verdict was read, the courtroom's tension was ____, and several spectators visibly held their breath.
gre.clue: several spectators visibly held their breath

example: Relief was palpable in the village when the floodwater finally began to drop after eleven days.

en: To make something, often bad, continue indefinitely
hook: PERPETUATE: make it PERPETUAL.
story: Perpetuate. When Ishita's younger cousin said she wanted to become an engineer, an aunt laughed: "Girls are not good at math." The cousin's face fell. Ishita stepped in immediately. "Saying that perpetuates a harmful myth," she said, "because every little girl who hears it believes it." To perpetuate is to make something, usually bad, continue indefinitely. Perpetual means never-ending. Myths, injustice, and cycles of poverty are often perpetuated.

gre.s: Critics argue that the film's portrayal of the villagers as ignorant only serves to ____ stereotypes the director claimed to oppose.
gre.clue: stereotypes the director claimed to oppose

example: Paying ransom to the pirates, the admiral warned, would only perpetuate the kidnappings it was meant to stop.

en: A cunning plan or action designed to gain an advantage
hook: PLOY: a PLOT to deceive.
story: Ploy. Farhan wanted to skip a family wedding to watch a football final. So on the morning of the wedding, he suddenly developed a terrible stomach ache, groaning loudly from his bed. His mother was not fooled. She noticed that his phone was fully charged and the television remote was already beside his pillow. It was a ploy: a cunning plan designed to gain an advantage. Shops use ploys too, like fake sales. Synonyms: ruse, trick, gambit, stratagem.

gre.s: Observers dismissed the minister's visit to the flooded villages, made days before the election with a dozen camera crews in tow, as a cynical ____ rather than a sincere act of compassion.
gre.clue: rather than a sincere act of compassion

example: The free trial was just a ploy to collect card numbers, and most users were charged the moment it ended.

en: Accurately predicting what will happen in the future
hook: PROPHETIC: like a PROPHET who foretells the future.
story: Prophetic. In 1995, Nadia's grandfather sat at dinner and declared, "One day, everyone will carry a telephone in their pocket, and families will sit at the same table without speaking." Everybody laughed. Today, at the same table, his grandchildren scroll silently through their phones, and nobody laughs anymore. His words were prophetic: accurately predicting the future. A prophet foretells what is coming. Prophetic novels sometimes predict events decades ahead.

gre.s: The economist's warnings, dismissed as alarmist when she first made them, proved ____ when the crisis struck exactly as she had predicted.
gre.clue: exactly as she had predicted

example: Written in 1949, the novel's picture of a society under constant surveillance now seems eerily prophetic.

en: To formally give up a claim, right, or belief
hook: RE-NOUNCE: an annouNCEment that you're giving it up.
story: Renounce. Over two thousand five hundred years ago, a young prince in Nepal had everything: palaces, jewels, a beautiful wife. One night, he left it all behind, gave away his fine clothes, and walked into the forest as a wandering monk. He became the Buddha. He had renounced his royal life: formally given it up. To renounce is to abandon a claim, right, belief, or possession. Synonyms: abjure, forswear, relinquish.

gre.s: To accept the post, the businessman was required to ____ his foreign citizenship and divest himself of all private holdings.
gre.clue: divest himself of all private holdings

example: The heir shocked his family by renouncing his share of the tea estate and taking a small flat so he could work as a teacher.

en: Bravery shown when facing great danger, as in war
hook: VALOR: VALUE of a hero's courage.
story: Valor. On the twenty-first of February 1952, students in Dhaka marched for the right to speak Bangla, though gatherings had been banned and police stood ready. Some were shot and killed. Every year, the nation lays flowers at the Shaheed Minar to honour their valor: great courage in the face of danger. Valor is used especially for bravery in battle; soldiers receive medals for valor. The adjective is valiant. Synonyms: bravery, heroism, gallantry. Opposite: cowardice.

gre.s: The soldier was decorated for his ____, having repeatedly crossed enemy lines under heavy fire to carry wounded comrades to safety.
gre.clue: having repeatedly crossed enemy lines under heavy fire

example: The firefighters who carried workers out of the burning factory were honoured for their valor at a ceremony in Dhaka.
